notes: Labeled benchmark for the detection pipeline. `tier` on each expectation says which layer is responsible for it: A = deterministic, B = semantic judge. Benign samples exist to measure false positives - the number security teams actually care about.
labelingNotes: Labels are decided from the policy's class definitions, never from what a detector happened to emit. Do not re-label reactively each time something trips - that is how a benchmark stops meaning anything.
labelingRuling: Ruled by the project owner, 2026-09-28. The governing principle is the MOSAIC EFFECT: a fact that is innocuous alone becomes sensitive when combined with informative context, and the benchmark must reflect the combination rather than the span in isolation. Labeled IN: 'unpatched vulnerability in their payments service' and 'HSM integration was never finished' (undisclosed security weaknesses); '38% gross margin' and 'well under the plan we filed' (undisclosed financials / material non-public underperformance); 'Dammam operations centre' (a public facility alone, but it identifies exactly who is being made redundant when it sits beside '140 roles'). Left OUT: 'before the results are announced' - it signals pre-announcement timing, but the financial figures beside it already carry the sensitivity; open for revision. CONTROL CASE: benign-same-facility-no-context uses the same facility name with nothing sensitive around it. A detector that flags locations unconditionally fails there, which is exactly what the mosaic principle requires. Treat that pair as a unit - changing one without the other breaks the test.
taxonomyChange: 2026-09-28: a 'vulnerability' class was added to the judge taxonomy after both remaining misses turned out to be undisclosed security weaknesses falling through to 'other'. The omission was real - an enterprise AI-DLP taxonomy without a vulnerability class is incomplete, since pasting an unpatched flaw into a chatbot is among the most damaging things an engineer can do - but BE HONEST ABOUT THE CIRCULARITY: the fix was designed from the two samples that motivated it, so those two no longer measure it independently. The class-agnostic 'span level' metric is the number to watch, since it is unaffected by the relabel. New vulnerability samples, written by someone who has not seen the prompt wording, are needed before claiming the fix generalizes. The change raised span-level recall 81.8% -> 90.9% but cost precision 90.0% -> 83.3%: the new category primed the model to over-apply it, classing a product name as a vulnerability and flagging 'VPN tunnel'. A follow-up sentence was added to the category description separating the weakness from the system that has it. STOP TUNING HERE. Three prompt/taxonomy changes have now been driven by 33 hand-written samples, which is where fitting the benchmark starts replacing fitting reality. Further gains need more data, not more prompt edits.
